how_customers_find_and_choose: Trade customers choose by relationship, reliability and credit terms; the first contact is often a phone call or chat from a referral
Shippers and retailers ask for live updates on where their goods are; a quick, clear status answer builds trust
Online business directories and map listings bring new business customers, especially for movers, couriers and warehouses
Reviews and word of mouth matter most to individuals and small shops booking movers or couriers
what_works_now: Sharing a status update in chat when goods are picked up, in transit and delivered, with a photo or proof where useful
Written quotes and booking confirmations with date, route, goods and terms
A saved list of regular customers with their usual routes, volumes and payment habits
Recording every delivery, delay and damage claim with a reference so disputes are settled from facts
Following up unpaid invoices on a set schedule, politely and in writing
A complete map listing with area covered, hours and contact for businesses that serve walk-in or local customers
Knowing vehicle or stock utilisation each week so empty runs and idle space are seen
outdated_or_weak: Chasing every customer by phone with no record of who asked what
Generic social media advice for a business whose buyers deal by relationship and contract
Quoting by gut with no record of past cost per route or per unit
Verbal agreements on credit terms with nothing written
Flyers and printed brochures as the main source of new business

PK: Cash on delivery and cash at the counter are still common; bank transfer and mobile wallet payments are now normal for many customers
Ramadan and the two Eids reshape demand, opening hours and staff availability every year
Summer heat, monsoon rain and power cuts affect operations and footfall
Customers often write in Urdu, Roman Urdu or a regional language, and chat is the usual first contact
Credit between traders is common and delayed payment is the main cash flow strain
Border, port and fuel cost changes quickly alter plans; holidays and strikes disrupt delivery schedules
Eid and wedding seasons raise demand for transport and wholesale
UAE: Customers are multilingual and expect quick replies in chat; card and tap payments are normal
Winter is the busy season; many residents travel in summer so demand can dip
Ramadan and Eid change hours and buying patterns; the licence a business holds decides what it may sell and advertise, so the owner checks that with the licensing body
A major trade and logistics hub: ports, free zones and re-export are central
Customs documents and trade licences are handled with the relevant authority or an agent; the owner confirms specifics with them
CA: Customers expect online booking or enquiry, card and bank e-transfer payment, and clear written confirmation
Long winters and a short summer peak shape outdoor and seasonal trades
English and French (in Quebec) matter, and many communities prefer their own language; consent for marketing messages and sales tax rules vary, so the owner checks them with a professional
Long distances and winter weather affect delivery times and costs
Cross-border trade rules and carrier requirements apply; the owner checks them with the authority or a broker

never_assume: Tracking technology on vehicles or goods
A customer list kept anywhere other than a phone or notebook
A website with a booking form
